usage: basic noun for a male person
noun + 이에요/예요; 남자 ends in a vowel, so 예요
with subject marker 가 after a vowel
남자 + 친구; with a space it means a friend who is male, while 남자친구 (one word) means boyfriend
examples: 남자 as the topic with 는
The tall man is my older brother.
남자 as the subject with 가
nuance: 남자 is the everyday word for a man or male and is neutral in tone. It is also used as a modifier, as in 남자 화장실 (men's restroom) or 남자 친구 (boyfriend). Be careful with spacing: 남자친구 written as one word often means a romantic boyfriend, while 남자 친구 with a space can just mean a friend who is male.
mistakes: Saying 남자이에요 after the vowel — it should be 남자예요.
Confusing 남자 (man) with 남편 (husband); a husband is 남편, not just any 남자.

usage: basic noun for a female person
with subject marker 가 after a vowel
여자 + 친구; with a space it means a friend who is female, while 여자친구 (one word) means girlfriend
examples: 여자 as the topic with 는
The women's clothing store is on the second floor.
여자 as the subject with 가
nuance: 여자 is the neutral everyday word for a woman or female and pairs with 남자 (man). Like 남자, it often works as a modifier: 여자 화장실 (women's restroom), 여자 친구 (girlfriend). Spacing matters: 여자친구 as one word usually means a romantic girlfriend, while 여자 친구 with a space can simply be a friend who is female.
mistakes: Writing 여자이에요 instead of the correct 여자예요.
Using 여자 when you mean 아내 (wife); a wife is 아내, not just any 여자.

usage: noun + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ
with subject marker 이 after a consonant
examples: You are an adult from age 19.
어른 as the topic with 은
nuance: 어른 means an adult or grown-up, the opposite of 아이 (child). In Korean culture it also carries a sense of respect, so 어른 can refer to one's elders or seniors whom you should treat politely. You will often hear 어른스럽다 (to be mature) built from this word.
mistakes: Saying 어른예요 — after the consonant ㄴ it must be 어른이에요.
Confusing 어른 (adult) with 노인 (elderly person); not every adult is old.

usage: with subject marker 가 after a vowel
examples: 아기 as the subject with 가
Our baby is one year old now.
아기 as the topic with 는
nuance: 아기 means a baby or infant and is a warm, affectionate word. It is sometimes shortened to 애기 in casual speech, though 아기 is the standard spelling. Parents also use 우리 아기 (our baby) as a term of endearment even for slightly older children.
mistakes: Writing 아기이에요 instead of the correct 아기예요.
Mixing up 아기 (baby) with 아이 (child); 아이 covers a wider age range than 아기.

usage: a young adult, usually in their 20s-30s
noun + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ
with subject marker 이 after a consonant
examples: That young man is very diligent.
청년 as the topic with 은
These days young people look for jobs.
That young man is my younger sibling.
nuance: 청년 refers to a young adult, typically someone in their twenties or thirties, and sounds a bit more formal than just 젊은 사람. It often appears in news and government programs like 청년 정책 (youth policy) or 청년 일자리 (youth jobs). It can describe a young man specifically, but is also used for young people in general.
mistakes: Saying 청년예요 — after the consonant ㄴ it must be 청년이에요.
Using 청년 for a teenager; teenagers are usually called 청소년, not 청년.

usage: noun + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ
with subject marker 이 after a consonant
examples: That elderly person exercises in the park.
노인 as the topic with 은
The elderly people are waiting for the bus.
This seat is a seat for the elderly.
nuance: 노인 is the standard word for an elderly person and is neutral in writing, such as 노인 복지 (welfare for the elderly). When speaking directly to or about an older person politely, Koreans usually prefer 어르신, which is more respectful than 노인. Use 노인 for general reference rather than as a direct form of address.
mistakes: Saying 노인예요 — after the consonant ㄴ it must be 노인이에요.
Calling an older person 노인 to their face; use 어르신 to be polite.

usage: the person who owns something or runs a place
noun + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ
with subject marker 이 after a consonant
examples: The owner of this shop is kind.
Who is the owner of this bag?
주인 with 이 in a question
nuance: 주인 means an owner or the person in charge of a place, like a 가게 주인 (shop owner). Combined with 집 it becomes 집주인, the standard word for a landlord. It can also mean host, and a pet's owner is often called 주인 by the pet's perspective, as in 강아지 주인 (the dog's owner).
mistakes: Saying 주인예요 — after the consonant ㄴ it must be 주인이에요.
Writing 집 주인 with a space when you mean landlord; the common word 집주인 is written together.

usage: with subject marker 가 after a vowel
examples: Those two people are a married couple.
That couple runs a cafe together.
부부 as the subject with 가
The newlyweds moved to a new house.
nuance: 부부 specifically means a married couple, a husband and wife as a unit. It is different from 커플, which is a borrowed word for a dating couple who are not necessarily married. Common combinations include 신혼부부 (newlyweds) and 노부부 (an elderly couple).
mistakes: Writing 부부이에요 instead of the correct 부부예요.
Using 부부 for a dating couple; an unmarried pair is 커플, while 부부 implies marriage.

usage: refers back to the person being discussed
noun + 이에요 after the consonant ㄴ
본인 + 확인; very common on forms
examples: The person must come in person.
본인 as the subject with 이
Only the person themselves can do this.
nuance: 본인 is a slightly formal word meaning oneself or the person in question, and it shows up constantly on official forms and at counters, as in 본인 확인 (identity check) or 본인 서명 (the person's own signature). It can mean my own self or that specific person, depending on context. In everyday casual talk people more often say 자기 or just use a name.
mistakes: Saying 본인예요 — after the consonant ㄴ it must be 본인이에요.
Overusing 본인 in casual chat; it sounds stiff, so use 저 or names with friends.

usage: 누군가 + 가; the subject marker is often added
examples: 누군가 used without an extra particle
Someone is knocking on the door.
I want to get help from someone.
nuance: 누군가 means someone or somebody, an unknown or unspecified person. It comes from 누구 (who) plus 가, and unlike plain 누구 it is a statement word, not a question. You can attach particles to it, as in 누군가가 (someone, subject) or 누군가에게 (to someone).
mistakes: Using 누군가 to ask a question; for questions use 누구 (Who is it? = 누구예요?).
Forgetting that you can still add 가/를; 누군가가 and 누군가를 are both correct.

usage: used with 도 or 나 to mean nobody / anybody
아무 + 도; always with a negative verb
examples: There is no one at home.
아무 ... 도 with a negative command
nuance: 아무 means anyone or any, but it almost never stands alone; it needs a partner particle. With 도 and a negative verb it means nobody or nothing (아무도 없어요 = no one is here), and with 나 it means anyone or anything at all (아무나 = anyone). Learn the set phrases 아무도, 아무나, 아무거나, and 아무 데나 together.
mistakes: Using 아무도 with a positive verb; 아무도 must go with a negative like 없어요 or 안 와요.
Saying 아무 alone to mean anyone; you need 아무나 or 아무도 to complete the meaning.

usage: an adult man, also used to address one
with subject marker 가 after a vowel
used to call a male worker or older man
examples: 아저씨 referring to a male worker
아저씨 as a form of address
That man told me the way.
아저씨 as the subject with 가
nuance: 아저씨 is the everyday word for a middle-aged or grown man, and it doubles as a friendly way to address a male stranger, shopkeeper, or driver, similar to mister. It is informal and warm, but calling a man who feels too young an 아저씨 can sound rude. Its female counterpart is 아주머니.
mistakes: Writing 아저씨이에요 instead of the correct 아저씨예요.
Calling a young man 아저씨; he may feel offended since it implies he looks middle-aged.

usage: an adult woman, also used to address one
with subject marker 가 after a vowel
the casual shortened form of 아주머니
examples: 아주머니 referring to a female worker
Ma'am, please give me some water.
아주머니 as a form of address
아주머니 as the subject with 가
nuance: 아주머니 is the everyday word for a middle-aged woman and a polite way to address a female stranger or shop worker, like ma'am. The shortened form 아줌마 is very common in speech but sounds more casual and can feel blunt, so 아주머니 is the safer choice. Its male counterpart is 아저씨.
mistakes: Writing 아주머니이에요 instead of the correct 아주머니예요.
Calling a young woman 아주머니 or 아줌마; it implies she looks middle-aged and may offend.

usage: noun + 이에요 after the consonant ㅅ
with subject marker 이 after a consonant
examples: 이웃 as the topic with 은
The neighbor shared rice cakes with us.
이웃 as the subject with 이
I get along well with my neighbors.
nuance: 이웃 means a neighbor, a person who lives close to you. It can refer to one person or neighbors in general, and you will see it in phrases like 이웃 사람 (neighbor) or 좋은 이웃 (a good neighbor). When you move in, greeting your 이웃 with 옆집 (the house next door) is a common cultural courtesy.
mistakes: Saying 이웃예요 — after the consonant ㅅ it must be 이웃이에요.
Pronouncing the final ㅅ as a clear s; before a vowel it links, so 이웃이 sounds like 이우시.
